n: The chapter opens by telling us the ending: the Lord is about to take Elijah to heaven in a whirlwind. Latter-day Saints understand Elijah was translated—taken without tasting death—so he could later return with a physical body to bestow priesthood keys.

f.g: probably a town in the hills near Bethel, not the Gilgal by the Jordan.

n: Three times Elijah urges Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha refuses with a solemn oath. His loyalty is being tested—and proven.
The prophetic community at Bethel knows Elijah will be taken today. Elisha knows too, and asks them to keep quiet—he doesn’t want to talk about it.

f.g: members of a prophetic fellowship or school.
from being your leader and master.

n: The second test: Elijah heads to Jericho, and Elisha again refuses to leave him.
The prophets at Jericho also know, and Elisha gives the same reply.
The third test: Elijah goes to the Jordan, and Elisha stays at his side.
Fifty prophets watch from a distance as the two stand by the river.
Elijah rolls up his cloak and strikes the water, which parts so they cross on dry ground—echoing Moses at the Red Sea and Joshua at this very river.
Elijah invites a final request. Elisha asks for a “double portion” of his spirit—the inheritance share of a firstborn son. He is asking to be Elijah’s true successor.

f.g: the firstborn son’s inheritance, twice the share of other sons.

n: Elijah says it is a hard request, beyond his power to grant. If Elisha is permitted to see him taken, that will be the sign the Lord has granted it.
As they walk and talk, a fiery chariot and horses separate them, and Elijah is carried up in a whirlwind. Fire and chariots symbolize God’s presence and heavenly armies.
Elisha cries out, calling Elijah “my father” and “the chariot of Israel and its horsemen”—meaning Elijah had been Israel’s true defense, worth more than an army. Elisha tears his clothes in grief.

f.w: the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof

f.g: tore them, a sign of mourning.

n: Elisha picks up Elijah’s fallen cloak—the very cloak once thrown over him at his call—and returns to the Jordan.
He strikes the water, calling, “Where is the LORD God of Elijah?” The waters part. The same God and the same power now rest on the new prophet.

f.w: Where is the LORD God of Elijah?
f.g: not doubt but an appeal: ‘Show Yourself now, O God of Elijah.’

n: The prophets watching recognize that Elijah’s spirit rests on Elisha, and they bow to him as their new leader.
They want to search for Elijah, thinking the Spirit may have dropped him somewhere. Elisha says no.
They pester him until he is embarrassed to keep refusing, so he lets them go. A three-day search finds nothing.

f.g: until he felt awkward refusing any longer.

n: When they return, Elisha gently reminds them he had told them not to go.
Elisha’s ministry of miracles begins. Jericho’s location is pleasant, but its water is bad and causes the land to be unfruitful.
Elisha asks for a new bowl filled with salt. A new vessel suggests something clean and set apart.
He throws the salt into the spring and declares that the Lord has healed the water. Salt was associated with covenant and purification.
The spring stayed pure “to this day.” A spring near ancient Jericho is still called Elisha’s Spring.
Near Bethel, the center of calf worship, a gang of young men mocks Elisha: “Go up, baldhead!”—possibly sneering at Elijah’s ascension and insulting God’s prophet.

f.g: Hebrew ne’arim qetannim: youths or young men, not toddlers.
perhaps mocking Elijah’s being taken up: ‘You go away too!’

n: Elisha curses them in the Lord’s name, and two bears maul forty-two of them. The story warns how seriously God regards contempt for His word and servants in that apostate city.

f.w: cursed them in the name of the LORD

n: Elisha travels to Mount Carmel, scene of Elijah’s great victory, and then to the capital, Samaria.
